passage:
Tuesday. Seema Masi phoned Leela, her voice cracking. A caller claiming to be from her bank had got her to send money, and now demanded "one more payment to release it". Leela's first thought was I told you about these calls, but what came out was, "Masi, don't send anything more. I'm coming over."

Thursday. At Masi's flat, Leela rang the bank's helpline on the number printed on the card, then sat beside her as she filed a report on the cyber portal. "I'm so stupid," Seema whispered. "They do this to clever people too," Leela said, and passed her the tea.

Sunday. Leela stuck a note on the fridge: Bank never asks for the code. Hang up. Call Leela. They practised a suspicious call together, laughing, and Masi hung up on the practice caller with a proud little nod.

qa.q: What did the caller demand on Tuesday?
qa.a: The caller demanded "one more payment to release it".

qa.q: How did Leela feel when Seema Masi phoned, and what shows it?
qa.a: Leela was probably frustrated at first, thinking "I told you about these calls", but concern won out and Leela said "Masi, don't send anything more. I'm coming over."

qa.q: How could Leela help Masi feel safe from now on?
qa.a: Keep the note on the fridge, practise hanging up on suspicious calls, use the bank's official number, and call Leela when unsure.

qa.q: How does Seema feel about herself after the scam, and what changes by Sunday?
qa.a: At first Seema calls herself stupid; by Sunday, after practising with Leela, she hangs up on the practice caller proudly and seems more confident.

grounding: Leela responds to a scammed elderly relative with compassion, not blame: stopping further payment, reporting it and building safety habits over several days.

passage:
I'm Madhav, and the call came from Gopika-mami at 9 p.m. She was crying. A man had said her grandson was in a police station and needed bail money sent right away. She had already sent twenty thousand and was about to send more.
My first thought, honestly, was: Mami, how could you? We've warned you. I bit it back.
"Mami, don't send anything else. I'm coming."
When I got there, she was sitting by the phone, ashamed. "I'm a foolish old woman."
"No. They're professionals. They fool clever people every day."
We called her bank to block further payments and dispute the transfer, then filed a report on the cybercrime helpline. Then I called her grandson, who was fine, at college.
Before I left, we wrote a card for her phone table: "Anyone asks for money urgently? Hang up. Call Madhav." She laughed, a little. Looking back, the card mattered more than my warnings ever had.

qa.q: How much had Gopika-mami already sent?
What was Gopika-mami feeling when Madhav arrived?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and foolish, crying and calling herself a foolish old woman.

qa.q: How did Madhav help without blaming?
qa.a: Madhav bit back the "I told you", reassured her, blocked further payments, reported the scam, and made a simple safety card for her phone table.

qa.q: How might the grandson feel learning about the call?
qa.a: The grandson may feel shocked and protective, and glad that Madhav stepped in quickly.

grounding: An elderly relative has just been scammed; the protagonist does not blame her, helps stop further payments, reports it, and builds a simple safety habit.

passage:
Supervisor's note, Thursday, 4 p.m.
Chinmay, junior analyst, came back from lunch pale and couldn't focus. When I asked, he said he'd paid a "customs fee" to someone claiming his parcel was held, and then paid again when they said it was "flagged". He kept saying, "I'm so stupid."
His teammate Mridul was already beside him. I watched Mridul pull up a chair and say, "No, you're not. These people are good at this." Mridul didn't mention that he had warned the team about this very scam last month.
Mridul helped Chinmay call the bank's official helpline to block his card and dispute the payment, then helped him file a complaint on the cybercrime portal. Afterwards, he showed Chinmay how to check a courier's real tracking site before paying anything.
I gave Chinmay the rest of the afternoon off. Mridul will present a short safety talk to the team on Monday.

qa.q: What did Chinmay pay the caller for?
qa.a: A "customs fee" for a parcel supposedly held, and then again when it was "flagged".

qa.q: What might Mridul have been feeling as he pulled up a chair?
qa.a: Mridul was probably concerned and sympathetic, choosing kindness over reminding Chinmay of the warning he had given.
He reassured him without blame, helped him block the card and dispute the payment, filed a cybercrime complaint with him, and showed him how to check a courier's real site.

qa.q: How might Chinmay feel after Mridul's help?
qa.a: Chinmay probably feels relieved and less alone, with a bit more confidence about spotting scams next time.

grounding: A colleague has just been scammed; the protagonist does not blame him, helps stop further payment, reports it and teaches a clear safety habit.
